modes.q: Why do multiple mass systems have multiple frequencies?
modes.a: Multiple mass systems have multiple frequencies because the masses can move in several different ways, called modes. In some modes the masses move together, and in others they move against each other. When the masses move against each other, the springs between them are stretched and compressed more, so more stiffness is working and that mode vibrates faster. So each mode has its own frequency, and a system with N masses has N modes and N frequencies.

modes.q: How many modes does a 3-mass system have?
modes.a: A 3-mass system has three modes. It has three because a system with N masses has N modes of vibration.

modes.q: Four masses are joined by springs between two walls. How many modes does the system have, and what are the masses doing in the lowest and highest modes?
modes.a: The system has four modes, because there is one mode for each mass. In the lowest mode, Mode 1, all four masses move in the same direction at the same time. In the highest mode, Mode 4, every mass moves opposite to its neighbors. So every spring is stretched and compressed, and the frequency is highest.

modes.q: Which mode of the 3-mass system has the highest frequency? Why?
modes.a: Mode 3 has the highest frequency. In Mode 3 the middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses, so every spring is stretched and compressed as much as possible. That puts the most stiffness to work, and more stiffness makes the system vibrate faster.

modes.q: Which mode of a 2-mass system has the lowest frequency, and why?
modes.a: Mode 1 has the lowest frequency. In Mode 1 the two masses move together, so the middle spring is carried along without stretching. Only the two outer springs are working, so Mode 1 has less stiffness than Mode 2 and vibrates more slowly.

modes.q: If you increase mass 2, what happens to the frequencies of each of the modes?
modes.a: If mass 2 increases, the frequencies of Mode 1 and Mode 3 go down, and Mode 2 stays the same. The middle mass moves in Mode 1 and in Mode 3, so making it heavier slows those modes and lowers their frequencies. In Mode 2 the middle mass does not move, and a mass that does not move has no effect on the frequency.

modes.q: In the 3-mass system, what happens to each mode if you make mass 1 (an outer mass) heavier?
modes.a: All three modes go down when mass 1 is made heavier. The outer mass moves in Mode 1, Mode 2 and Mode 3, and a heavier mass that is moving lowers the frequency. No mode leaves an outer mass still, so none of the three frequencies stays the same.

modes.q: In a 2-mass system, what happens to each mode if you make the middle spring stiffer?
modes.a: Mode 1 stays the same and Mode 2 goes up. In Mode 1 the masses move together, so the middle spring is never stretched and its extra stiffness does nothing. In Mode 2 the masses move against each other, so the middle spring is stretched and compressed, and the extra stiffness raises the frequency.

modes.q: What do you get when you have an infinite number of masses and springs?
modes.a: An infinite number of masses and springs gives a string, such as a guitar or piano string. Every small piece of a string has mass, and every small piece stretches the way a spring does. So a string vibrates in modes the same way a chain of masses does, only with infinitely many of them. When the masses and springs are spread over a surface instead of a line, the result is a membrane, such as a drum or the vocal folds.

modes.q: What happens to the frequency of a single mass on a spring if you make the spring stiffer? If you make the mass heavier?
modes.a: A stiffer spring raises the frequency, and a heavier mass lowers it. A stiffer spring pulls the mass back toward equilibrium with more force, so the mass turns around sooner. A heavier mass is harder to start and stop, so each back-and-forth cycle takes longer and the frequency goes down.

springiness.q: This is Mode 5 of a string fixed at both ends. Circle the areas where there is the most springiness.
springiness.a: The most springiness is at the two fixed ends and at the four points where the string crosses its middle line, so six places should be circled. The string does not move at those points, but the pieces on either side move in opposite directions. So the string there is stretched and compressed the most. The tops of the five bumps have the most motion and the least springiness, so they are not circled.

springiness.q: This is Mode 3 of a string fixed at both ends. Where is the most springiness, and where is the most motion?
springiness.a: The most springiness is at the two fixed ends and at the two points where the string crosses its middle line, four places in all. The string does not move at those points, so it is stretched and compressed the most there. The most motion is at the tops of the three bumps, where the string swings the most and is hardly stretched.

springiness.q: This picture shows Mode 4 of a building. Circle the areas where there is the most springiness.
springiness.a: The most springiness is at the fixed base and at the three points where the building crosses its resting position, so four places should be circled. Those points do not move, but the parts above and below them move in opposite directions. So the structure there stretches and compresses the most. The free top moves the most and is the least springy, so it is not circled.

springiness.q: This diagram shows Mode 2 of a building. Where is the most springiness?
springiness.a: The most springiness is at the fixed base and at the one point above it where the building crosses its resting position. Those two points do not move, so the structure there is stretched and compressed the most. The free top moves the most, so it is the least springy.

springiness.q: If we increase the stiffness and mass of the string at the boxed location (where Mode 3 crosses its middle line and Mode 4 is at the top of a bump), what happens to Mode 3 and Mode 4's frequencies, and why?
springiness.a: Mode 3's frequency goes up and Mode 4's frequency goes down. In Mode 3 the boxed spot does not move but is stretched the most, so the added mass does nothing and the added stiffness raises the frequency. In Mode 4 the boxed spot moves the most and is not stretched, so the added mass lowers the frequency and the added stiffness does nothing.

springiness.q: The box is moved to a spot where Mode 3 is at the top of a bump and Mode 4 crosses its middle line. Mass and stiffness are added there. What happens?
springiness.a: Now Mode 3 goes down and Mode 4 goes up. In Mode 3 the spot moves the most and is hardly stretched, so the added mass lowers the frequency. In Mode 4 the spot does not move but is stretched the most, so the added stiffness raises the frequency.

springiness.q: If we increase the mass and stiffness of the building at its very top, what happens to the frequency of Mode 4, and why?
springiness.a: The frequency of Mode 4 goes down. The top of the building is the free end, so in every mode it moves the most and is hardly stretched. The added mass counts there and lowers the frequency. The added stiffness does nothing, because nothing is stretching at the top.

springiness.q: If we increase the mass and stiffness of the building at its very base, what happens to the frequency of Mode 4, and why?
springiness.a: The frequency of Mode 4 goes up. The base is the fixed end, so it never moves but is always stretched and compressed. The added mass does nothing there because the base does not move, and the added stiffness raises the frequency.

springiness.q: In Mode 3 of a string fixed at both ends, point B does not move and point C is at the bottom of a bump. What happens to Mode 3 if you add a small weight at B? At C? If you stiffen the string at B?
springiness.a: A weight at B leaves Mode 3 the same, because B does not move in Mode 3. A weight at C lowers Mode 3's frequency, because C swings the most and the extra mass counts there. Stiffening the string at B raises Mode 3's frequency, because B is where the string stretches the most.

springiness.q: The same spot B is moving in Mode 1. Does a weight at B change Mode 1's frequency?
springiness.a: Yes, a weight at B lowers Mode 1's frequency. In Mode 1 the whole string is one bump, so the spot at B is moving. Extra mass at a moving spot slows the vibration, so the frequency goes down.

harmonics-formants.q: A string is fixed on both sides. If Mode 1 has frequency 200 Hz, what frequency does Mode 5 have?
harmonics-formants.a: Mode 5 has a frequency of 1000 Hz. In a string fixed at both ends, each mode is a whole-number multiple of the first. Mode 5 contains five copies of Mode 1, so its frequency is five times 200 Hz.

harmonics-formants.q: A string fixed at both ends has Mode 1 at 150 Hz. What are Modes 2 and 3? If one end is freed and Mode 1 stays at 150 Hz, what are Modes 2 and 3 now?
harmonics-formants.a: Fixed at both ends, Modes 2 and 3 are 300 and 450 Hz, which are two and three times 150. Fixed at one end and free at the other, Modes 2 and 3 are 450 and 750 Hz, which are three and five times 150, because only the odd multiples occur. So the fixed-fixed modes are 150 Hz apart, and the fixed-free modes are 300 Hz apart.

harmonics-formants.q: Why are the frequencies of fixed-fixed vibratory systems spaced the way they are?
harmonics-formants.a: The frequencies of a fixed-fixed system are evenly spaced whole-number multiples of the first, because every mode has to fit a whole number of half-waves between the two still ends. The first mode is half a wave, going from no motion at one end to the most motion in the middle and back to no motion. Mode 2 fits two half-waves into the same length, so it vibrates twice as fast. Mode 3 fits three, so it vibrates three times as fast, and the spacing stays even.

harmonics-formants.q: Why are the formants of a fixed-free system 1, 3, 5, etc. multiples of the base frequency?
harmonics-formants.a: The formants of a fixed-free system are odd multiples because every mode must start still at the fixed end and end with the most motion at the free end. The basic piece is a quarter-wave packet, which runs from no motion at the fixed end to the most motion at the free end. One extra packet would leave a still point at the free end, which cannot happen, so packets are added two at a time. That gives one, three, five and seven packets, so the frequencies are odd multiples of the base frequency.

harmonics-formants.q: If F1 is 500 Hz, what are F2 and F3?
harmonics-formants.a: F2 is 1500 Hz and F3 is 2500 Hz. The air in the vocal tract is a fixed-free system, so its formants are odd multiples of the first. So F2 and F3 are three times and five times 500 Hz, not two and three times.

harmonics-formants.q: What aspect of speech has the properties in the fixed-free question?
harmonics-formants.a: The formants of the air in the vocal tract have these properties. The air is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips. So its frequencies of vibration, the formants, are odd multiples of the first formant.

harmonics-formants.q: What aspect of speech has frequencies at whole-number multiples, and why?
harmonics-formants.a: The harmonics of the vocal folds are at whole-number multiples. The vocal folds are a membrane held in place along their edges, so they behave like a system fixed at both ends. So each mode is a whole number of copies of the first.

harmonics-formants.q: What in speech is a building analogous to, and why does the analogy hold?
harmonics-formants.a: A building is analogous to the air in the vocal tract. Both are fixed at one end and free at the other. The building is fixed to the ground and free at the top, and the air is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips. Because the ends match, both have springiness at the fixed end, the most motion at the free end, and frequencies at odd multiples of the first.

harmonics-formants.q: How is a building different from the air in the vocal tract?
harmonics-formants.a: A building is designed to sway only in Mode 1, but the air in the vocal tract vibrates in all of its modes at once. Engineers avoid the higher modes because they would move floors in opposite directions and could break the structure. In speech, speaking changes the mass and stiffness of the air at different locations, so the formants move.

harmonics-formants.q: Draw the spectrum for a string fixed at both ends with Mode 1 at 200 Hz, up to Mode 6.
harmonics-formants.a: The spectrum has six evenly spaced spikes at 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 and 1200 Hz, one for each mode. Frequency goes along the horizontal axis and amplitude goes up the vertical axis. The spikes are evenly spaced because a string fixed at both ends has its modes at whole-number multiples of Mode 1. If the modes are equally strong, the spikes can be drawn the same height.

harmonics-formants.q: Draw the spectrum for a fixed-free system with Mode 1 at 200 Hz, up to Mode 4.
harmonics-formants.a: The spectrum has spikes only at the odd multiples, 200, 600, 1000 and 1400 Hz. A fixed-free system has no even multiples, because an even number of quarter-wave packets would leave a still point at the free end.

harmonics-formants.q: If the vocal folds have their base frequency, F0, at 150 Hz, draw the spectrum for the first 5 harmonics.
harmonics-formants.a: The spectrum has spikes at 150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz, with frequency along the bottom and amplitude going up. The vocal folds are a membrane fixed along its edges, so their harmonics are whole-number multiples of F0. So the spikes are evenly spaced, 150 Hz apart.

constrictions.q: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and I raise the formant a great deal, what must be true of air motion versus springiness at this location?
constrictions.a: At that location the air must be very springy and hardly moving in that mode. A constriction adds both mass and stiffness, and the formant went up, so the added stiffness is what counted. Stiffness only counts where the air is compressed and expanded. The added mass did nothing, because the air there was not moving.

constrictions.q: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and I lower the formant a great deal, what must be true at this location?
constrictions.a: At that location the air must be moving a lot and hardly compressed in that mode. The formant went down, so the added mass is what counted, and mass only counts where the air is moving. This is what happens at the lips for /u/.

constrictions.q: A classmate says more mass lowers the frequency and more stiffness raises it, so a constriction always cancels out. What is wrong with this argument?
constrictions.a: The argument is wrong because, in any one mode, only one of the two changes matters at most locations. If the air at the constriction is mostly moving, it is not being compressed, so only the extra mass counts and the formant goes down. If the air there is mostly compressed, it is not moving, so only the extra stiffness counts and the formant goes up. That is why the same constriction can push F1 and F2 in opposite directions.

constrictions.q: Why is the air in the vocal tract a fixed-free system? Say which end is which.
constrictions.a: The glottis end is the fixed end, and the lip end is the free end. The glottis end is closed off by the vocal folds, so the air there cannot move and can only be compressed and expanded. The lip end is open, so the air there moves freely in and out without being compressed against anything.

constrictions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in dune, and why?
constrictions.a: Both F1 and F2 go down in dune. Lip rounding creates a constriction at the free end, where the air moves the most in every mode. So the added mass counts in both Mode 1 and Mode 2, and extra mass at a moving location lowers the frequency.

constrictions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in dean, and why?
constrictions.a: In dean, F1 goes down and F2 goes up. The constriction is about two-thirds of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1 the air there is moving, so the added mass lowers F1. In Mode 2 the air there is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F2.

constrictions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in Don, and why?
constrictions.a: In Don, F1 goes up and F2 goes down. The constriction is about one-third of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1 the air there is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F1. In Mode 2 the air there is moving, so the added mass lowers F2.

constrictions.q: A new constriction is placed deep in the throat, one-fifth of the way from the glottis, where the air is compressed in both Mode 1 and Mode 2. What happens to F1 and F2?
constrictions.a: Both F1 and F2 go up. The location is near the fixed end, where the air is compressed in both modes. So the added stiffness is what counts in both modes, and extra stiffness raises the frequency.

constrictions.q: Why does rounding the lips lower every formant?
constrictions.a: Rounding the lips lowers every formant because the lips are the free end of the vocal tract. The free end is a location of maximum motion in every mode. So a constriction there adds mass where the air is moving, and that lowers every formant. Adding mass at the top of a building lowers every mode for the same reason.

source-filter.q: What does the source supply and what does the filter do in speech?
source-filter.a: The vocal folds are the source, and they supply the harmonics, which are whole-number multiples of F0. The air in the vocal tract is the filter. Its formants make the harmonics near them louder and the ones far from them weaker. So the source decides which frequencies are present, and the filter decides which of them are loud.

source-filter.q: Two vowels are said at the same pitch. What is the same and what is different in their spectra?
source-filter.a: The harmonics are the same, but the heights of the harmonics are different. The harmonics match because the vocal folds vibrate at the same F0 for both vowels. The heights differ because each vowel has its constriction in a different place, so the formants move and the envelope changes.

source-filter.q: Why are a toddler's vowels hard to identify?
source-filter.a: A toddler's vowels are hard to identify because a toddler has a very high F0, so the harmonics are spaced far apart. Few harmonics fall near each formant, and a formant can fall between two harmonics, so the envelope is hard to see. The formants are still there, but there are too few harmonics to reveal them.

source-filter.q: If the vocal folds become tighter, what happens to F0 and to the spacing of the harmonics?
source-filter.a: F0 goes up, and the harmonics are spaced farther apart. Tighter vocal folds are stiffer, and more stiffness raises the frequency. The harmonics are multiples of F0, so when F0 goes up they spread farther apart.

spectrogram.a: A spectrogram lines up many spectra side by side over time. Time runs along the horizontal axis and frequency runs up the vertical axis. The darkness of each spot shows how much amplitude there is at that frequency and time. The formants appear as dark bands, so you can follow them as they rise and fall, for example F1 rising and F2 falling from /i/ to /a/.

spectrogram.q: How is a spectrum different from a spectrogram?
spectrogram.a: A spectrum shows one instant, and a spectrogram shows how the spectrum changes over time. A spectrum has frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. A spectrogram has time on the horizontal axis and frequency on the vertical axis, with amplitude shown as darkness. Real speech is always changing, so a spectrogram shows the formants moving.

spectrogram.q: A speaker starts on schwa and switches to another vowel. F1 goes down and F2 goes up. Which vowel? What if both go down?
spectrogram.a: When F1 goes down and F2 goes up, the vowel is /i/ as in dean, and the two bands move apart. When both F1 and F2 go down, the vowel is /u/ as in dune, because lip rounding lowers every formant.

spectrogram.q: Describe the spectrogram of a speaker going from schwa to the vowel of Don.
spectrogram.a: F1 goes up and F2 goes down, so the two lowest dark bands move toward each other. The constriction for Don is one-third of the way from the glottis. The air there is compressed in Mode 1, so the added stiffness raises F1. The air there is moving in Mode 2, so the added mass lowers F2.

spectrogram.q: Why do listeners hear na when the m of ma is joined to the a of na?
spectrogram.a: Listeners hear na because the information about the consonant is carried mostly by the vowel that follows it. After n, one formant of the vowel drops, and after m, that formant stays flat. So the a from na still signals n. Listeners decide which consonant they heard during the vowel, after the consonant is over.

network-forward.q: If an activation of 1.57 feeds the done output through a weight of positive 0.1, what happens to the probability of done if the weight goes up? If the activation goes up?
network-forward.a: The probability of done goes up in both cases. The contribution to the done output is the activation times the weight, and both are positive. So raising either one makes the product larger and pushes done up. Only the signs matter, so no multiplication is needed.

network-forward.q: What happens to the probability of done if that same weight were negative and the activation went up?
network-forward.a: The probability of done goes down. A positive activation times a negative weight is negative. So a larger activation makes the contribution more negative and pushes the done output down.
No, it is not a valid probability distribution. The numbers add up to 1.1, and a probability distribution must add up to exactly 1.

network-forward.q: The first of five categories is correct. Write the desired output.
network-forward.a: The desired output is 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. It puts all of the probability on the correct category, so every other category gets zero.

network-forward.q: The desired output over done, dune, dean, Don, Dan is 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, and the network outputs 0.10, 0.15, 0.60, 0.10, 0.05. Which vowel was said, which did the network guess, and what is the loss?
network-forward.a: Don was said, and the network guessed dean, because dean has the largest probability, 0.60. The loss is a number that measures how far the computed output is from the desired output. For example, it measures how much probability the network put on dean where there should be a 0.

network-forward.q: What does Linear mean in the network code?
network-forward.a: Linear means the layer computes inner products. Each neuron multiplies each incoming number by its weight and adds the results. A Linear layer does nothing else, so its outputs are just those sums.

backprop.q: In what order are the weights updated?
backprop.a: The last set of weights is updated first, and the first set of weights is updated last. This order works because each layer's update reuses what was already worked out for the layers after it.

backprop.q: Why does backpropagation start at the end?
backprop.a: Backpropagation starts at the end because the last weights are the simplest problem. The last weights affect the output probabilities, which are the decision, directly, so it is easy to tell whether raising or lowering each one makes the loss go up or down. A weight from the input to the first hidden layer affects the first, second and third hidden layers before the output, so changing it is a very complex problem that contains the problem of changing the last weights. Following dynamic programming, the simplest problem is solved first, and its answer makes each harder problem easier until the most complex one is solved.

backprop.q: What two methods together train the network's weights?
backprop.a: The two methods are stochastic gradient descent and backpropagation. Backpropagation works backward from the error to find which way each weight should change. Stochastic gradient descent then moves each weight a small step in that direction.

backprop.q: Backpropagation is made of what two parts?
backprop.a: Backpropagation is made of stochastic gradient descent and dynamic programming. Stochastic gradient descent nudges each weight a small step in the direction that lowers the error. Dynamic programming sets the order, from the last weights back to the first.

backprop.q: Which part of training is the SGD part, and which is the dynamic programming part? What are the small problem and the big problem?
backprop.a: The SGD part is the adjusting, where each weight takes a small step in the direction that lowers the error, and the learning rate sets the size of that step. The dynamic programming part is the order of assigning blame. The last layer goes first, and each layer's blame is reused for the layer before it. The small problem is the blame of the last layer's weights, and the big problem is the blame of the early weights.

backprop.q: The network said done but the answer was dean. Should a last weight that pushes done up go up or down? Why?
backprop.a: That weight should go down. The probability of done is too high, because the desired output for done is zero. So lowering a weight that pushes done up shrinks its contribution and pulls the probability of done toward zero.

backprop.q: If the network already makes the right decision on a recording, what does it learn from it?
backprop.a: It learns nothing from that recording, because there is no error to correct. This can be a problem, because a network can keep getting the right answers by memorizing its data without learning the pattern underneath.

pytorch.q: How many hidden layers does this network have: Linear(2, 3), Linear(3, 2), Linear(2, 4), Linear(4, 5)?
pytorch.a: The network has three hidden layers, with three, two and four neurons. It has five layers in all, the input layer, three hidden layers and the output layer, but only four Linear lines. That is because the input layer does no processing, so it gets no line, and the last line is the output layer.

pytorch.q: Write the code for the network with an additional hidden layer of 3 neurons right before the output layer, and adjust the other layers.
pytorch.a: Keep the first three lines, change the old last line from Linear(4, 5) to Linear(4, 3), and add a new last line, Linear(3, 5). The network becomes Linear(2, 3), Linear(3, 2), Linear(2, 4), Linear(4, 3), Linear(3, 5). This works because every layer still takes in exactly as many numbers as the layer before it produces.

pytorch.q: Add a hidden layer of 6 neurons right after the input instead. What changes?
pytorch.a: The first line becomes Linear(2, 6), and a new second line, Linear(6, 3), feeds the old first hidden layer. The rest stays the same, so the network is Linear(2, 6), Linear(6, 3), Linear(3, 2), Linear(2, 4), Linear(4, 5).

pytorch.q: A network is written Linear(4, 3), Linear(3, 5), Linear(5, 2), Linear(2, 4). How many hidden layers, inputs and outputs does it have?
pytorch.a: It has three hidden layers, with 3, 5 and 2 neurons. It takes 4 numbers as input and has 4 output neurons, so it decides among 4 categories.

pytorch.q: How many hidden layers does a network have if its code is Linear(2, 3), Sigmoid, Linear(3, 2), Sigmoid, Linear(2, 4), Sigmoid, Linear(4, 5)?
pytorch.a: It still has three hidden layers. Sigmoid lines are not layers, because they only apply the sigmoid to the layer before them. So only the four Linear lines count, and the last one is the output layer.

pytorch.q: What do the import lines do, and what does Sequential mean?
pytorch.a: The import lines bring the torch library into Python, so the programs for inner products and backpropagation do not have to be written by hand. Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers, one after another. Each layer takes its input from the layer before it.

pytorch.q: What happens if the learning rate is raised from 0.1 to 0.3?
pytorch.a: The network learns faster, but its accuracy goes down. A larger learning rate takes bigger steps, so the network approaches the answer quickly but keeps overshooting it.

pytorch.q: Two learning curves differ only in learning rate. One rises fast and jumps around, and the other rises slowly and smoothly. Which used the larger learning rate?
pytorch.a: The one that rises fast and jumps around used the larger learning rate. Bigger steps get near the answer quickly but overshoot, so that curve jumps around. Smaller steps are slower, so the other curve rises slowly but smoothly.

sigmoid.q: Where does the idea of the sigmoid come from?
sigmoid.a: The idea of the sigmoid comes from biology. Lord Edgar Adrian discovered that real neurons are nearly digital, either firing or not firing, and he won the Nobel Prize in 1932. The sigmoid copies this by turning any inner product into a number between 0 and 1. So a neuron is nearly off or nearly on.

sigmoid.q: A hidden neuron's inner product is minus 2. Is its sigmoid activation closer to 0 or 1, and what does that mean?
sigmoid.a: Its sigmoid activation is closer to 0, because the inner product is negative. So the neuron is mostly off and fires only rarely.

sigmoid.q: If one input to that neuron goes up through a positive weight, what happens to its linear activation and its sigmoid activation?
sigmoid.a: Both the linear activation and the sigmoid activation go up. A larger input times a positive weight raises the inner product. The sigmoid always rises when its input rises, so the neuron fires more often.

sigmoid.q: What is the sigmoid activation if the linear activation is exactly 0?
sigmoid.a: The sigmoid activation is 0.5, which is halfway between off and on. So the neuron is half active.

sigmoid.q: How does the sigmoid match human perception?
sigmoid.a: The sigmoid matches perception because some very different things are perceived as the same, and some very similar things are perceived as different. The flat parts of the sigmoid give the same output for very different inputs, such as minus 100 and minus 1000. The steep middle gives very different outputs for two nearly equal inputs on either side of zero.

training.q: Why does accuracy start at 20 percent?
training.a: Accuracy starts at 20 percent because the network starts with random weights and knows nothing. So its guesses are no better than chance. Guessing at random among five vowels is right one time in five, which is 20 percent.

training.q: Why does accuracy start at 10 percent for a network with ten output categories?
training.a: Accuracy starts at 10 percent because a network with random weights guesses no better than chance. A random guess among ten categories is right one time in ten, which is 10 percent.

training.q: Why does the vowel network level off near 40 to 45 percent instead of 100 percent?
training.a: The network levels off near 40 to 45 percent because the real formant data for the five vowels overlap a great deal. Many recordings with nearly the same F1 and F2 belong to different vowels. For a point in the middle of the overlap even a person would have to guess, so no network can classify those points reliably.

training.q: Ten training runs start from different random weights. What happens?
training.a: All ten runs end at about the same accuracy, even though they take different paths. Some jump up early and some stay at chance longer, because stochastic gradient descent involves chance along the way. The end point is still the same.

lead-up.q: How does the all-or-none behavior of neurons connect to the sigmoid?
lead-up.a: The all-or-none behavior of neurons and the sigmoid are the same idea. A real neuron is either firing or not firing. The sigmoid turns an inner product into a number near 0 (off) or near 1 (on), with a steep change in between, so an artificial neuron behaves the same way.

lead-up.q: What do parallel and distributed mean in Parallel Distributed Processing?
lead-up.a: Parallel means many neurons calculate their activations at the same time. Distributed means the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons, so it is not stored in one place.

lead-up.q: What does a single neuron take in and give back? What about a neural network?
lead-up.a: A single neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number, the inner product of the inputs and their weights. A neural network repeats the inner product layer after layer. So a network takes in one vector and gives back a vector of decisions.

lead-up.q: Why can't the vowel network model a sentence or speech over time?
lead-up.a: The vowel network cannot model speech over time because it takes one static vector and makes one decision. That vector is F1 and F2 from one moment. Speech changes all the time, and a sentence is many words one after another, so it needs a network that works through a sequence.

lead-up.q: What makes Jordan's network recurrent, and why did he build it?
lead-up.a: Jordan's network is recurrent because it sends its own output back into part of its input. It copies the output into the state units, so what it produced at one moment helps predict the next. Jordan built it because speech production changes over time, as features such as nasality and lip rounding switch on and off.

lead-up.q: How is a recurrent network different from an nn.Sequential network?
lead-up.a: A Sequential network passes the input through the layers once, from the input to the output, and makes one decision. A recurrent network loops its output back into its input, so it works through a sequence step by step.

lead-up.q: How does GPT use the same idea as Jordan's network?
lead-up.a: GPT also feeds its own output back into its input. It predicts the next word, adds that word to the prompt, and predicts again, so it produces text one word at a time.

heads-layers.q: What are heads, and how do they relate to layers?
heads-layers.a: A head is one expert, a set of weights that gives its own opinion on how to improve the vectors. Heads sit side by side inside each layer, and the layer combines all of their opinions into improved vectors. Layers go one after another from the input to the output, so each layer improves the vectors again.

heads-layers.q: In the classroom of experts, what are the classes and what are the students?
heads-layers.a: The classes are the layers, because you visit them one after another. The students in each class are the heads, because each one gives a separate opinion at the same time. You combine those opinions before moving on to the next class.

heads-layers.q: Which gives an LLM depth and which gives it width, heads or layers?
heads-layers.a: Layers give an LLM depth, because they are rounds of improvement that come one after another. Heads give it width, because many of them work side by side inside the same layer.

heads-layers.q: An LLM has 5 layers with 4 heads in each layer. How many heads does it have, and which of them work at the same time?
heads-layers.a: It has 20 heads, because each of the 5 layers has 4. The 4 heads inside one layer work side by side at the same time. The layers come one after another, so layer 2 works on the vectors that layer 1 improved.

heads-layers.q: The LLM predicts bark instead of barks after "the dog that my parents ... ". Which weights change?
heads-layers.a: The weights of every head in every layer change. Backpropagation assigns each weight its share of the blame for the wrong prediction. Each weight is then adjusted a little, so the next prediction is closer to barks.

heads-layers.q: Where is the knowledge of an LLM stored?
heads-layers.a: The knowledge of an LLM is stored in its weights. Each head is a set of weights, so the knowledge is spread across all the heads in all the layers. The vowel network's knowledge is stored in its weights in the same way.

llm-sequences.q: What is the difference between the input and output of the vowel network and those of an LLM?
llm-sequences.a: The vowel network takes one vector, F1 and F2, and decides among five categories. An LLM takes many vectors in sequence, such as the words so far, and decides among a whole vocabulary for the next item.

llm-sequences.q: An LLM is given 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth. Name three things the vectors can stand for.
llm-sequences.a: The vectors can stand for the words of a sentence, the frames of a spectrogram or the patches of an image. They can also stand for the amino acids of a protein. The same kind of prediction works for all of them, because the LLM only sees lists of numbers.

llm-sequences.q: What does the sixteenth vector look like, and does it add up to anything?
llm-sequences.a: The sixteenth vector is a probability distribution over what could come next. It has one number for each possible next item, such as each English word. Because it is a probability distribution, its numbers add up to one.

llm-sequences.q: Why is the next word barks and not bark in "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, ... "?
llm-sequences.a: The next word is barks because it goes with the singular word dog, no matter how many words come in between. This holds even when the plural word parents comes in between. To predict barks, an LLM has to use a word far back in the sequence, and it learns to do this from data by computing inner products layer after layer.
An LLM can hallucinate because it predicts from past data. When it meets something its data does not cover, its prediction can turn into a guess, so it can make things up.

gestalt-cloze.q: Describe the Gestalt principle of closure, and how an LLM uses it to learn.
gestalt-cloze.a: Closure is completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished, such as seeing a triangle where none is drawn or seeing a broken circle as whole. An LLM learns by doing the same kind of completion. It predicts the missing next piece of a sequence again and again, and it corrects its weights when it is wrong.

gestalt-cloze.q: What is a cloze test, and why is an LLM's training like one?
gestalt-cloze.a: In a cloze test, words are removed from a text and people fill them in, so knowledge is tested by completing a sequence. An LLM is trained by filling in the next word over and over. So for an LLM, completion is what knowledge is.

gestalt-cloze.q: Why do people see a triangle in the Gestalt figure?
gestalt-cloze.a: People see a triangle because they complete the missing parts of a familiar pattern, even though no triangle is drawn. This completion is the Gestalt principle of closure.

recurrent-dynamical.q: Why is an LLM called a dynamical system?
recurrent-dynamical.a: An LLM is called a dynamical system because it works by feeding a rule its own output again and again. A dynamical system is a rule fed its own output repeatedly, starting from initial conditions. In an LLM the input vectors are the initial conditions, and each layer applies its weights to turn them into better vectors. So the depth of the layers plays the role of time.

recurrent-dynamical.q: In the harmonic oscillator, which two numbers update, and in what order?
recurrent-dynamical.a: Position x and velocity v update, and they take turns. First the new x is calculated from the old v, and then the new v is calculated from the new x. Repeating this step by step makes x trace out a cosine.

agentic.q: What is an agentic system, in terms of LLMs? Describe the example system.
agentic.a: An agentic system is a graph of LLMs, each with its own job, connected so that one LLM's output becomes the next one's input. In the example, one LLM outlines, one writes, one critiques, one revises and one produces the final version. The critic and the reviser form a loop, so the draft keeps going back until the critic is satisfied or the limit is reached.

agentic.q: What does the critic loop do, and what does it prevent that was common in earlier LLMs?
agentic.a: The critic loop sends the draft back until the critic is satisfied, so errors are caught and fixed before they are presented. It prevents hallucination, which was a common problem in earlier LLMs.

agentic.q: What would happen if the critic LLM were removed?
agentic.a: Without the critic, the draft would go straight from writing to the final answer without being checked. So more made-up statements would reach the user, because the critic loop is what greatly reduced hallucination.

agentic.q: What is the difference between Software 2.0 and Software 3.0?
agentic.a: In Software 2.0, a neural network is trained on input and output data, so the program is its weights. In Software 3.0, an agentic system builds and runs the program from plain English instructions, as in vibe coding.

phonotactics.q: Which could be English words: blick, bnick, sblat, splat, dlag, lisk, lisb, lapm, lamp? For each one that could not, name the problem.
phonotactics.a: Blick, splat, lisk and lamp could be English words. Bnick, sblat and dlag are impossible because bn, sb and dl cannot start a syllable. Lisb and lapm are impossible because sb and pm cannot end a syllable.

phonotactics.q: Each of these starts an English word: pl_, st_ and th_. What could come next, and what could not?
phonotactics.a: After pl only a vowel can come, as in play, so a consonant such as n cannot. After st a vowel or r can come, as in star and street, but l and k cannot. After th, r, w or a vowel can come, as in three, thwart and thin, but l and n cannot.

phonotactics.q: After which start is the next-letter distribution flatter, ra_ or skr_? Why?
phonotactics.a: The distribution is flatter after ra. After a vowel almost any letter can come next, so the probability is spread over many letters. After skr only a vowel can come, so the probability piles onto a few vowels and the distribution is sharply peaked.

phonotactics.q: Why is Atlantic an English word but tlantic impossible?
phonotactics.a: Atlantic is a possible word because its t and l are on opposite sides of a syllable break, so each syllable follows the rules. In tlantic, tl would have to start a syllable, and English does not allow tl at the start of a syllable.

phonotactics.q: Could ngop be an English word? Could flim?
phonotactics.a: Ngop could not be an English word, but flim could. The sound ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but it can never start one. Flim is possible because fl is an allowed onset, as in flat, and im is an allowed ending.

phonotactics.q: Why does a GPT trained only to guess the next letter end up knowing English syllable structure?
phonotactics.a: A GPT ends up knowing syllable structure because the patterns of English syllables decide which letters can come next. Its predictions can only improve by matching those patterns. So the knowledge ends up in the shape of its probability distributions, which are flat after a vowel and peaked after a start such as skr.

phonotactics.q: Which letter cannot come next after sp_ at the start of a word: l, r, n or a?
phonotactics.a: N cannot come next. After sp only l, r or a vowel can come, as in split, spring and spa, because spn is not an allowed English onset.

phonotactics.q: Which letter cannot come next after k_ at the start of a word: a, n or t?
phonotactics.a: T cannot come next. After k a vowel or n can come, as in knee, but kt cannot start an English syllable.

phonotactics.q: What can come next after b_ or f_ at the start of a word, and what cannot?
phonotactics.a: After b or f, only r, l or a vowel can come next, as in bring, black, frog and flat. N cannot come next, because bn and fn cannot start an English syllable.

phonotactics.q: What can come next after sh_ at the start of a word?
phonotactics.a: After sh, only a vowel or r can come next, as in ship and shrimp. Shr is the only consonant cluster that English allows there.

phonotactics.q: What can come next after skr_?
phonotactics.a: After skr, only a vowel can come next, as in scream and scrap. Skr already fills the onset, so no other consonant can be added.

phonotactics.q: Why are lfat, hepl and lapm impossible when flat, help and lamp are words?
phonotactics.a: Lfat, hepl and lapm are impossible because the order of a cluster is a mirror image around the vowel. In flat and help the l sits right next to the vowel, and in lamp the m does. Each impossible twin puts the wrong consonant next to the vowel, so it breaks the mirror order.

phonotactics.q: Is ship a consonant, vowel, consonant word even though it has four letters?
phonotactics.a: Yes, ship is a consonant, vowel, consonant word. The pattern is about sounds, not letters, and sh is one sound. So ship is the consonant sh, the vowel i and the consonant p.
